Next, we recall the graph of $y = \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x.$

![](images/07/074a330c55b63458fe94ed36b0c569ecfc6ce8fd839b8566f1dd589440c59c69.png)

$$

$$

$$
-3\cdot \lim_{x\to-\infty} \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x = -\infty.
$$

We can evaluate this limit using direct substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}({3}^{2x}+{2}^{3x}+1) & ={3}^{2(1)}+{2}^{3(1)}+1 \\  & =9+8+1 \\  & =18\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Evaluating Using Direct Substitution

:question/problem: Given that ${lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{4}^{x}-c}{3\cdot {2}^{x}}=2$, what is the value of constant $c?$
:question/worked-solution:
We can evaluate this limit in terms of the constant $c$ using direct substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{4}^{x}-c}{3\cdot {2}^{x}} & =\frac{{4}^{0}-c}{3\cdot {2}^{0}} \\  & =\frac{1-c}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we know that the above limit is equal to $2,$ we can equate the above with $2,$ and then solve for $c:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-c}{3} & =2 \\ 1-c & =6 \\ -c & =6-1 \\ c & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Since we know that the above limit is equal to $4,$ we can equate the above with $4,$ and then solve for $c:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{32}{9+c} & =4 \\ 9+c & =8 \\ c & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Evaluating Infinite Limits of Exponential Functions

:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {4}^{x} &=-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{4}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the graph of $y={4}^{x}.$

![](images/db/db8c8ab9423f9c56a6eb4c4602bb8c2e162e07c9a2e4ac99f7670343146ce13a.png)

From the graph, we see that the function decreases to zero as $x$ decreases. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{4}^{x}=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{4}^{x}=\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)\cdot 0=0.
$$

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Evaluating Infinite Limits Using the Laws of Exponents and the Algebra of Limits

:question/worked-solution:
From the previous part, we know that

$$
\widehat{s}(t)=\frac{1}{1-2t}.
$$

We can use the laws of exponents and the algebra of limits to rewrite the given limit, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to -\infty }{e}^{\widehat{s}(t)} & ={lim}_{t\to -\infty }{e}^{\frac{1}{1-2t}} \\  & ={e}^{\,\,{lim}_{t\to -\infty }\frac{1}{1-2t}} \\  & ={e}^{0} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{t\to -\infty }{e}^{\widehat{s}(t)}=1.
$$

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Evaluating Infinite Limits Using the Laws of Exponents and the Algebra of Limits

:question/worked-solution:
From the previous part, we know that

$$
\widehat{p}(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3t+1).
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\widehat{q}(t)={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3t+1)}=3t+1.
$$

We can use the laws of exponents and the algebra of limits to rewrite the given limit, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \infty }{e}^{\widehat{q}(t)} & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }{e}^{3t+1} \\  & ={e}^{\,\,{lim}_{t\to \infty }(3t+1)} \\  & =\infty \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{t\to -\infty }{e}^{\widehat{q}(t)}=\infty .
$$

:question/worked-solution:
We can evaluate this limit using direct substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}{3}^{3x+8} & ={3}^{3(-2)+8} \\  & ={3}^{-6+8} \\  & ={3}^{2} \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$
